headline: I tried to film a 'latent' roast of my family dinner but it accidentally became a self-help seminar
body:
I grew up thinking that true comedy was about cutting deep and leaving no survivors, so I decided to turn my sister’s engagement dinner into an 'India’s Got Latent' style roast. I had my ring light set up, a notebook full of brutal observations about my brother-in-law’s choice of footwear, and a dream of becoming the next viral sensation. But the second I started my set, my aunt actually started crying—not from laughter, but because she felt 'truly seen' by my critique of her inability to delegate potato chopping.

Instead of the edgy, high-octane verbal warfare I expected, the room turned into a profound therapy session. My uncle, who I was planning to eviscerate for his questionable investments, stood up and thanked me for the 'emotional breakthrough.' Apparently, when you apply the raw intensity of a professional roast to your own kin, people don't get offended; they just get introspective. I tried to pivot back to a joke about his hairline, but he just patted my back and said, 'Thank you for acknowledging my internal struggle, son.'

I went home with zero usable footage for my channel and a newfound sense of family cohesion that I absolutely did not want. The comments section of my life is currently being flooded with 'this is so wholesome' instead of the toxicity I carefully curated. I’ve realized that if you strip away the filtered, polished veneer of modern performance, you aren't left with pure comedy—you’re just left with a group of people who are suddenly ready to discuss their feelings. It’s disgusting, and frankly, it’s ruined my career as a part-time antagonist.
caption: When the roast goes wrong and everyone starts hugging. Who knew comedy could be this dangerous? #Comedy #FamilyDinner #LatentRoast #WholesomeFail (satire)
